The idea is about the close sitting above the open: a gap that is large relative to the day's range, not just the close-to-close move. The plainest reading is the log of (close − open)/high − 1, so I'll start there with a 5-day mean.

The plain close-to-open gap is essentially the same information as the close-to-close return, and it carries no incremental content at all — that's expected because a single-day gap is just a re-expression of the day's return. The idea says a big drop yesterday should be followed by a bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return is low. I'll start with the simplest form: minus one times yesterday's return, which is exactly "how much did it fall yesterday".

The plain version is fully absorbed by the short-term reversal style — incremental IC is exactly zero, and the sign flips between periods. So the raw size of yesterday's drop carries no new information; what may survive is its *unusualness*: a coin that normally moves a lot but fell a lot yesterday, versus one that fell little. I'll express the drop as a z-score of the 20-day return, so the factor rises only when yesterday's fall is large relative to that coin's own normal move.

The z-score version is also flat (incremental −0.0006, t = −0.6) and its sign flips across periods, so "unusual fall" carries no new information either. The last thing I can try is the same quantity in units of the coin's own typical daily move, which is a different way of saying "fell a lot relative to its normal size".

That is a clear pattern, not a single failed test: the bounce after a fall is already fully explained by the short-term reversal style, and the "unusualness" and "relative to its own size" refinements add nothing.

I'll submit the simplest form, which is the one least entangled with those styles, keeping the direction the idea states (bigger fall, higher factor value).
